title: PRD (Draft) — Status Page Transparency Upgrades
content:
Doc status: DRAFT (pre-Confluence)
Owner: Paula Mendes (PM)
Product lead: Marissa Cole
SRE sponsor: Sean Gallagher
SRE delivery lead: Rafael Mendes

Last updated notes:
- This is the working PRD draft intended to become the Confluence page “Status page transparency upgrades — PRD”.
- Draft includes open questions and partial copy. Do not treat as policy until Security/Compliance review is complete.


1) Summary / Problem Statement
Redwood’s public status page is currently too coarse for how customers experience incidents in production. Customers frequently see “API degraded” when the real impact is narrower (e.g., streaming disconnects, embeddings-only latency, rerank error spikes, one model family, or one region’s capacity). This creates:
- Confusion (“what’s actually impacted?”)
- Extra support load and escalations during incidents
- Customer self-mitigation delays (fallbacks, region pinning, retry strategy)
- Enterprise trust issues (especially Dedicated and Private customers with SLAs)

This PRD proposes a set of upgrades to make customer-facing incident communication more accurate, timely, and actionable:
1) Increase status page component granularity
2) Standardize incident update templates + update cadence guidance
3) Publish consistent post-incident summaries aligned with internal postmortems (within disclosure boundaries)
4) Add light tooling/automation to reduce manual burden and keep status page in sync with incident lifecycle


2) Goals / Success Criteria
Primary goals (customer-facing outcomes):
- Customers can quickly determine scope: which product surfaces are affected (streaming vs non-streaming; embeddings; rerank; console; control planes) and which regions are affected.
- Customers receive updates that are timely, consistent, and include actionable mitigation/workaround guidance where possible.
- Customers can expect a post-incident summary for high-severity incidents, in a consistent format and timeline.

Operational goals (internal outcomes):
- Reduce oncall cognitive load and “blank updates” during high-pressure incidents.
- Reduce support/CS escalations driven by unclear status messaging.
- Improve status page accuracy via clearer mapping between internal alerts and public components.

Draft success metrics (to refine with SRE + Support ops):
- Time to first public status update (TTFU): median and p90 for Sev1+ incidents
- Update timeliness: % incidents where next update time is stated and met (within tolerance window)
- “What’s impacted?” support contacts: count of support tickets / Slack escalations during incidents referencing unclear impact scope
- Customer satisfaction signal: CSAT trend for incident-related tickets; qualitative CSM feedback
- Post-incident summary SLA: % Sev1/Sev0 incidents with summary published within target window


3) Non-Goals
- Not changing Redwood’s internal incident process fundamentals (roles, severity definitions, oncall rotations), beyond what’s needed for external comms.
- Not publishing sensitive details (customer names, exploit paths, vulnerability-like technical steps, provider contractual details).
- Not guaranteeing new hard SLA commitments via status page wording.
- Not building a brand-new status page platform. We will work within the current vendor/tooling and add only necessary integrations.


4) Users & Use Cases
User types:
A) External customers (developers, platform teams)
- Need quick assessment of impact to their integration and what actions they can take.
- Need confidence that “Resolved” means a stable state, and understand when monitoring is still ongoing.

B) Support / Customer Success / GTM
- Need a single source of truth to send customers during incidents.
- Need consistent language that matches what SRE is posting (avoid divergence between ticket macros and status updates).

C) SRE / Oncall engineers
- Need an easy, consistent workflow to publish high-quality updates quickly.
- Need guardrails to prevent low-information updates and reduce debates over wording/phase.

D) Product/Console team (internal)
- Needs alignment between status page components and Console UX / docs (glossary; “How to read our status page”).


5) User Stories
External customer stories:
- As a customer, I want to know if the issue is limited to Streaming so I can switch to non-streaming responses temporarily.
- As a customer, I want to know if only Embeddings are affected so I can keep chat features online.
- As a customer, I want to know which region is impacted so I can route traffic or pin to an alternate region.
- As a customer, I want to know whether errors are due to capacity/routing constraints vs platform outage so I can adjust retry/backoff and fallback model strategy.
- As a customer, after a major incident, I want a brief summary explaining impact, timeline, high-level cause category, and what Redwood is doing to prevent recurrence.

Support/CS stories:
- As Support, I want to reference consistent mitigation guidance (“retry with exponential backoff”, “use fallback model X”, “pin region Y”) that matches the status page language.
- As a CSM, I want post-incident summaries I can forward to enterprise customers without requesting internal postmortems.

SRE/oncall stories:
- As oncall, I want a guided status update workflow with phase-based templates so I can post quickly and consistently.
- As incident commander, I want the system to prompt for next update time and ensure we’re not missing the cadence expectations.
- As SRE, I want an incident-to-component mapping that matches alerts/metrics and reduces confusion on what to mark impacted.


6) Requirements (Draft)
6.1 Component granularity (status page taxonomy)
We will publish a customer-comprehensible set of components that map to how customers experience the platform.

Draft component buckets (names subject to design review):
- Hosted API (Core Requests) — general request/response availability excluding streaming-specific behavior
- Streaming — streaming token responses (SSE/websocket behavior as applicable), disconnects, keepalive issues
- Embeddings — embeddings endpoints performance/availability
- Rerank — reranking endpoints performance/availability
- Console — UI availability and critical operational workflows (e.g., model configuration visibility)
- Dedicated Control Plane — provisioning/management operations for Dedicated
- Private Control Plane — provisioning/management operations for Private
- Serving (by region) — us-east, us-west, eu-west (initial scope)
- Capacity & Routing — partial degradations primarily due to throttling/429s/capacity constraints (TBD whether this is separate or a label)

Notes:
- Avoid internal jargon in public component names (“scheduler”, “router”, “orchestrator”). Prefer customer framing (“Capacity & Routing”).
- Regions should be used when impact is clearly localized. Do not “over-regionalize” incidents with global symptoms.

Acceptance criteria (product-facing):
- Component list is understandable to a customer without internal context.
- Components cover the majority of incident patterns we’ve seen in past ~90 days (SRE to validate).
- Each component has a short definition + examples of partial impact (docs/glossary).

6.2 Incident communication templates
We will standardize the content structure for each incident phase:
- Investigating / Initial
- Identified
- Monitoring
- Resolved

Template requirements:
- Every update must include at least one of: impact, mitigation/workaround, next update time (guardrail).
- Every update must include (where known): affected components + region scope.
- Use approved uncertainty language (e.g., “We are investigating reports of…”, “We believe the impact is limited to…”, “We have not confirmed…”).
- Include customer actions when safe and accurate: retry guidance, backoff, fallback models, region pinning.

6.3 Update cadence guidance
We will publish internal guidance (not necessarily public) on expected update cadence by severity.

Draft guidance (for discussion):
- Sev0/Sev1: first update within 10–15 minutes; subsequent updates every 30 minutes (or sooner on major changes). Must always set next update time.
- Sev2: first update within 30 minutes; updates every 60–120 minutes depending on progress.

Notes:
- Cadence guidance must be achievable; avoid commitments that will be regularly missed.

6.4 Post-incident summaries (customer-facing)
For Sev1/Sev0 incidents, Redwood will publish a customer-facing post-incident summary with a consistent format.

Required sections:
- What happened (1–3 sentences)
- Customer impact (who/what was affected; scope; what was not affected)
- Timeline (UTC)
- Root cause category (high level, non-sensitive)
- Mitigation and resolution
- Prevention / follow-ups (high level)

Draft SLA:
- Publish within 3 business days for Sev1/Sev0.

Disclosure requirements:
- Must comply with external comms approval policy (Security/Legal constraints).
- Never include customer-specific info or exploit-like technical detail.

6.5 Tooling & workflow automation
We will add lightweight automation to reduce manual steps:
- Incident-bot prompts for phase-based status updates + required fields
- Sync incident lifecycle state changes → draft status page updates (human review before publish)
- Post-incident summary workflow: create stub doc, pre-fill incident timeline references, reminders at T+1 and T+3 business days


7) UX / Content Design Notes (Draft)
- Component naming should prioritize clarity over internal accuracy.
- Include a short public doc: “How to read our status page” with examples of what each component means.
- Ensure we do not imply that “Dedicated Control Plane degraded” means customer inference is down; be explicit.
- Provide consistent troubleshooting guidance aligned with templates (retry/backoff, fallbacks, region pinning, checking rate limit headers).


8) Rollout Plan
Phase 0 — Alignment (Week 1)
- Finalize taxonomy proposal + mapping principles (SRE + Product + Support)
- Security/Compliance review of disclosure boundaries
- Confirm status page platform capabilities/constraints (components, subcomponents, history/backfill)

Phase 1 — Pilot (Weeks 2–3)
- Pilot new component taxonomy on a limited surface:
  - Hosted API Serving (region components) + Streaming
- Use new update templates for all Sev1+ incidents in pilot scope
- Start collecting baseline metrics (TTFU, update cadence compliance)

Phase 2 — Expand components + docs (Weeks 3–6)
- Add Embeddings, Rerank, Console components
- Publish “How to read our status page” doc + component glossary
- Support macros updated to match templates

Phase 3 — Post-incident summary workflow (Weeks 4–8)
- Begin publishing customer-facing summaries for Sev1/Sev0
- Evaluate SLA compliance and adjust reminders/ownership model

Release / change management:
- Announce internally (oncall training + runbook updates)
- External announcement (status page + docs) once taxonomy is stable


9) Measurement Plan (Detailed)
Baseline (before rollout):
- Past 30–60 days incidents: TTFU, number of updates per incident, % updates that include a “next update” time
- Support tickets tagged “incident status confusion” (Support ops to define)

During pilot:
- Daily check-in: any incident comms friction points; template edits tracked in a changelog

After rollout (4–6 weeks post):
- Compare TTFU, update completeness, number of escalations, and qualitative feedback
- Review sample of incidents for comms quality rubric:
  - Clear impact scope
  - Correct components
  - Actionable mitigation included when possible
  - No disclosure violations


10) Dependencies
- SRE: component taxonomy + mapping rules, severity/cadence alignment, oncall training
- Incident-bot / tooling: implementation of prompts, required fields, and draft sync
- Docs: public docs updates (“How to read our status page”, glossary)
- Security/Compliance: approval policy for external comms and summary content
- Status page platform: ability to add components, region breakdown, and not break historical incident pages


11) Risks & Mitigations
Risk: Over-granular components lead to confusion or inconsistent usage
Mitigation: Start with a manageable taxonomy; provide examples and a decision tree; training + runbook.

Risk: Missed cadence commitments undermines trust
Mitigation: Internal guidance only (initially); require next update time; measure and adjust.

Risk: Post-incident summaries become too slow or too vague
Mitigation: Use a lightweight standardized format; enforce ownership; reminders; security review checklist.

Risk: Disclosure mistakes (sharing sensitive provider/security details)
Mitigation: Clear “never disclose” list; approval workflow; Security consulted on ambiguous cases.


12) Open Questions (Needs resolution before Confluence publication)
1) Component taxonomy final names:
- Do we expose “Capacity & Routing” as a standalone component, or treat it as a tag/label applied to regional serving components?
- Do we need separate components for “Model Catalog” vs “Serving” or is that too internal?

2) Region scoping rules:
- When do we mark “Serving (us-east)” vs global “Hosted API” vs both?
- If a routing service is global but only us-east capacity is constrained, how do we message clearly?

3) Post-incident summary SLA:
- Is 3 business days the right target for Sev1/Sev0? Do we commit to anything for Sev2?

4) Approval workflow:
- Who is the final approver for post-incident summaries (SRE lead vs incident commander vs Security)?
- Do we require Security review for every summary or only for specific root cause categories?

5) Tooling scope:
- Which parts of incident-bot automation are must-have for v1 (templates + next update time) vs v1.5 (draft sync + summary stub)?

6) Console surface:
- Do we need any Console UI changes as part of this project (e.g., link from Console → status page component glossary), or keep Console changes to docs only?


13) Appendix — Draft Copy Snippets (Working)
Investigating (draft):
“We’re investigating reports of increased errors affecting [components] in [region(s)]. Some customers may see [symptom]. Next update by [time UTC].”

Identified (draft):
“We’ve identified the cause as [high-level category]. We are applying mitigation [X]. Impact remains [scope]. Next update by [time UTC].”

Monitoring (draft):
“Mitigation has been applied and we’re seeing recovery in [metrics]. We’re monitoring to confirm stability. Next update by [time UTC].”

Resolved (draft):
“This incident is resolved. [Brief fix]. If you continue to experience issues, contact Support with request IDs and timestamps.”


Notes to self / TODO (PM):
- Pull 3–5 concrete incident examples from SRE and rewrite them using new templates to validate readability.
- Confirm with Docs (Elliot) where “How to read our status page” will live and what the public commitments are.
- Align with Support ops (Dev Patel) on ticket tagging for measurement.
- Confirm whether Dedicated/Private status visibility differs (some customers may rely on private comms) and how we handle hybrid incidents.
